For now it makes more sense to either burn hydrogen or use electricity to make hydrocarbons from atmospheric CO2. Today's batteries don't have the energy density required.

You can make an electric semi-tractor, and you can make an electric ducted fan-type airplane engine, now. The biggest problem is the power source: the sorts of batteries we now use just don't provide the sort of energy density, i.e. joules-per-kilogram, that a tank of fossil fuel and a heat engine will provide.

That said, there are other ways of producing electricity besides obtaining it from a charged-from-the-line battery. Fuel cells, burning alcohol or hydrogen, actually exceed the energy density of a tank of fossil fuel and a heat engine. Fuel cells are expensive and wear out quickly, but there's a lot of money to be made by solving those problems, so they'll get solved.

And in the longer term, there are other sources of energy than chemical reactions. The biggest problem with a nuclear-powered "battery" is that you can't turn it off. It's producing energy, lots of it, whether or not any is needed. However that problem isn't insuperable.

And "quantum nucleonic" power sources, although at the moment more in the realm of speculation than of engineering, can be turned on and off. Someone has to figure out how to produce nuclear isomers, and the right ones, in commercial quantities, but there's a lot of money in that, too.

But remember about batteries: the more energy is stored in a battery, the more like a bomb the battery becomes. In all these instances the trick is to make a high-capacity battery that won't release all its energy at once. That's kind of tricky. (Remember high-capacity laptop batteries six or eight years ago?)

So we're kind of stuck with fossil fuels for the moment. But not forever.
